lec05kp20-u01-p1-nf-lec05-kp20-recipe-1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-recipe|The three-step recipe of the kernel trick: (1) rewrite the algorithm so that it uses only inner products; (2) replace every inner product by a kernel K; (3) write the solution as a linear combination of the training points. The weight vector never has to be computed; K must satisfy the Mercer condition. Kernelization = replacing the inner products of an algorithm that uses only inner products by a kernel function, giving a non-linear version in the original space.

lec05kp20-u01-p2-bridge.name: u01-p2-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p2-bridge.text: Kernelization takes three steps: only inner products, inner products to kernels, a linear combination. Can the simplest classifier, the distance to the two class means, be kernelized?

lec05kp20-u01-p2-nf-lec05-kp20-kmean-1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-kmean|The Euclidean (nearest-mean) classifier: a new point goes to the class whose mean it is closer to. Left: a sketch of the kernel space with the two classes, their means μ₁, μ₂ and the distances from the new point φ(x) to both means. Right: when the squares are expanded and the two distances subtracted, ‖φ(x)‖² cancels; class 2 is closer exactly when ⟨φ(x),μ₂−μ₁⟩>θ with θ=(‖μ₂‖²−‖μ₁‖²)/2; with kernels ⟨φ(x),μ_k⟩ is the average of the kernel values K(x,x_i) of class k and ‖μ_k‖² the average of the kernel values inside the class. The rule: choose class 2 when the average kernel value of class 2 minus that of class 1 exceeds θ. The difference from a Parzen estimate is the extra threshold θ.

lec05kp20-u01-p4-title.text: The kernel perceptron: mistake counters α replace the weights and the discriminant is only kernels

lec05kp20-u01-p4-bridge.name: u01-p4-bridge
lec05kp20-u01-p4-bridge.text: Comparison on concentric rings shows a new kernel does not remove the threshold. Can a more learning-like algorithm, the perceptron, be kernelized too?

lec05kp20-u01-p4-nf-lec05-kp20-kperc-1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-kperc|The kernel perceptron: the linear perceptron updates w←w+y_t φ(x_t), w₀←w₀+y_t each time a point is misclassified (y_t g(x_t)≤0); the final w is therefore a linear combination of training points, and with α_i the number of times point i was misclassified, w=Σα_i y_i φ(x_i), w₀=Σα_i y_i; the discriminant g(x)=Σα_i y_i K(x_i,x)+Σα_i y_i never needs the weight vector. Algorithm: all α are 0; sweep the training points round by round, computing g(x_i) from the current α; if y_i g(x_i)≤0 then α_i←α_i+1; stop when a whole round has no mistakes. Convergence: after the mapping to a high dimension, by Cover's theorem the data are linearly separable with high probability.

lec05kp20-u01-p7-nf-lec05-kp20-losses-1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-losses|The four losses against the margin value z=y·g(x) (z>0 right, z≤0 wrong): hinge max(0,1−z), exponential e^{−z}, logistic ln(1+e^{−z}), 0/1. lec05kp20-u01-p8-nf-lec05-kp20-logup-1.name: fig:lec05-kp20-logup|The step of the 0/1 loss (1 for z≤0, else 0), the logistic ln(1+e^{−z}) and the logistic divided by ln2. steps.label: The kernel trick beyond SVM
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp20 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic, with the terms defined inside the same figure. 7 main pages plus 3 extension pages (not timed); sections 7 and 8 of the lecture are merged into page 7. All experiments (the Euclidean classifier on concentric rings, the hand trace, the rounds and accuracy of the perceptron, the loss table) were designed for this lecture and generated by code; rerunning them reproduces the lecture's numbers item by item. The source provides the three-step kernelization recipe, the kernelized Euclidean classifier and its relation to Parzen, the update and discriminant of the kernel perceptron, the four losses and their uses, and the 'how to remember' summary. English version.

steps.label: Three-step recipe
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP20, following KP19, where the kernel let the SVM lift to a higher dimension. This unit asks whether other algorithms that use only inner products can be lifted like the SVM, and the answer is yes. First one term: kernelization replaces the inner products of an algorithm that uses only inner products by a kernel function, giving a non-linear version in the original space. The recipe has three steps: first, rewrite the algorithm so that it contains only inner products; second, replace every inner product by a kernel K; third, write the solution as a linear combination of the training points. So the weight vector never has to be computed. The kernel K must satisfy the Mercer condition, as in KP19. How to remember: these three steps are the general recipe of the kernel trick, not an SVM patent. Next, the following page turns to Euclidean classifier.

steps.label: Euclidean classifier
steps.speakerNotes: The kernelization on the previous page takes three steps: only inner products, inner products to kernels, a linear combination. This page asks whether the simplest classifier, comparing the distances to the two class means, can be kernelized. The Euclidean classifier, also called nearest mean, averages the training points of each class and gives a new point to the class whose mean it is closer to. Kernelizing it means doing the same thing in the mapped kernel space. The left panel is a sketch of the kernel space: the two classes, their means mu 1 and mu 2, and the distances from the new point phi of x to both means. The right panel gives the three key steps of the derivation: first, expand the squares and subtract the two distances, and the squared length of phi of x appears in both and cancels; second, class 2 is closer exactly when the inner product of phi of x with mu 2 minus mu 1 exceeds the threshold theta, theta being half of the squared length of mu 2 minus that of mu 1; third, with kernels the inner product becomes the class average of K of x and x i and the squared length becomes the average of the kernel values inside the class. The rule: choose class 2 when the average kernel value of class 2 minus that of class 1 exceeds theta. The difference from a Parzen estimate is the extra threshold theta. Next, the following page turns to Comparison on rings.

steps.label: Comparison on rings
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page, Euclidean classifier. Comparison on concentric rings: the same data, four Euclidean (nearest-mean) classifiers. The linear kernel gets 488 right, 48.8%; the quadratic kernel 938, 93.8%; the Gaussian kernel with the threshold theta 974, 97.4%; and without theta only 798, 79.8%, which is 176 points fewer and 17.6 percentage points lower. The experiment was designed for this lecture: two concentric rings, uniformly random angles, normally distributed radii with standard deviation 0.25; 60 training points per class, 120 in all, seed 1; 500 new points per class, 1000 in all, seed 2; the quadratic kernel x transpose z plus 1, squared, and the Gaussian kernel with gamma 0.5. Why kernelization helps: in the original space both class means are near the origin, so comparing distances to the means can hardly tell inside from outside; the kernel gives similarities after the mapping without computing high-dimensional coordinates. Theta makes up for the difference between the two classes: the in-class kernel averages are about 0.212 for the outer ring and 0.477 for the inner ring, so 2 theta is about 0.265 and theta about 0.1325. Only this one data set was drawn, with no repetition, which does not mean every data set ranks the same. Next, the following page turns to Kernel perceptron.

steps.label: Kernel perceptron
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed the Euclidean classifier is simple, and the Gaussian kernel already reaches 97.4%. This page asks whether a more learning-like algorithm, the perceptron, can be kernelized too. First recall the linear perceptron: every time a point is misclassified, that is y t times g of x t is at most 0, update w to w plus y t times phi of x t and w0 to w0 plus y t, starting from zero. An update just adds one training point, so the final w is a linear combination of the training points. Let alpha i be the number of times point i was misclassified: w is the sum of alpha i y i phi of x i and w0 is the sum of alpha i y i. Substituting into the discriminant g of x leaves only kernels: the sum of alpha i y i K of x i and x, plus the sum of alpha i y i. The kernel perceptron is the perceptron whose counters alpha i replace the weight vector. The algorithm in four steps: all alpha are 0; sweep the training points round by round and compute g from the current alpha; add 1 to alpha i on a mistake; stop when a whole round has no mistake. Convergence: after the mapping to a high dimension the data are linearly separable with high probability, by Cover's theorem. Next, the following page turns to Hand trace.

steps.label: Hand trace
steps.speakerNotes: The kernel perceptron on the previous page uses mistake counters alpha instead of weights. This page works through a small example designed for this lecture and computes every point's discriminant: four points, x1 equal to 1,0 and x2 equal to −1,0 are +1, x3 equal to 0,1 and x4 equal to 0,−1 are −1, with kernel K equal to x transpose z plus 1, squared; this is XOR-type data, which no line can separate. First the kernel matrix G: for example K of x1 and x1 is 2 squared, which is 4; K of x1 and x3 is 1; K of x1 and x2 is 0. The trace round by round: in round 1, point 1 has g equal to 0, y times g equal to 0, a mistake, and alpha becomes 1,0,0,0; point 2 is right; point 3 has g equal to 2 and y times g equal to −2, a mistake; point 4 is also a mistake and alpha becomes 1,0,1,1. In round 2, point 1 is right, point 2 has g equal to −3, a mistake, and alpha becomes 1,1,1,1, points 3 and 4 are right. In round 3 all four are right, with g equal to 2, 2, −2, −2, and the algorithm stops. The final g of x is 2 times x1 squared minus x2 squared; 2,0 gives +8 and 0,2 gives −8. Next, the following page turns to Ring experiment.

steps.label: Ring experiment
steps.speakerNotes: The hand-traced XOR-type example on the previous page stops after three rounds with alpha equal to 1,1,1,1. This page asks how many rounds it takes on more realistic concentric rings and how accurate it is. The experiment was designed for this lecture and generated by code: concentric rings generated as in the previous experiment, with standard deviation 0.15, rings apart, and 0.25, rings touching; 60 training points per class with seed 1 and 500 new points per class with seed 2; a Gaussian kernel with gamma 0.5; each round sweeps the 120 training points in order and the linear perceptron runs at most 500 rounds; only this one data set was drawn. The result: with standard deviation 0.15 the kernel perceptron stops after 8 rounds, 13 points have alpha above 0, and 982 new points are right, 98.2%; with 0.25 it needs 428 rounds, 22 points, 956 right, 95.6%; the linear perceptron still makes mistakes after the full 500 rounds in both cases and gets 500 new points right, 50.0%. The figure shows the number of mistakes in each round against the log-scaled round number. When separable it is guaranteed to stop in finitely many steps, but when the two classes are close the rounds grow from 8 to 428. With the same standard deviation 0.25 and the same training data, gamma equal to 0.1, 2, 8 need 191, 571, 175 rounds to stop, so the rounds are also sensitive to gamma. Next, the following page turns to Loss functions.

steps.label: Loss functions
steps.speakerNotes: On the previous page the linear perceptron still errs after 500 rounds while the kernel perceptron stops when the rings are apart. This page asks what separates the perceptron from the SVM: look at the loss each one minimises, and whether the four losses punish a wildly wrong point equally. First two terms. The margin value is z equal to y times g of x: z above 0 is right, z at most 0 is wrong, and the more negative the more wildly wrong. A loss function gives every z a penalty, and it sets the personality of the algorithm. The four: hinge, the maximum of 0 and 1 minus z, used in the soft-margin SVM; exponential, e to the minus z, used in AdaBoost, to be discussed in KP25; logistic, ln of 1 plus e to the minus z, the negative log-likelihood of the logistic probability model; and 0/1, which counts 1 when z is at most 0 and 0 otherwise, counting mistakes directly but not differentiable. The values: at z equal to −2 hinge is 3, exponential 7.389, logistic 2.127 and 0/1 is 1; at z equal to 0 they are 1, 1, 0.693, 1; at z equal to 2 they are 0, 0.135, 0.127, 0. The exponential is steepest on the negative side: at z equal to −2 its penalty is 7.389 divided by 3, which is 2.46 times that of hinge. This means a wildly wrong point, noise or an outlier, is punished especially hard by the exponential loss, which is AdaBoost's drive to concentrate on hard points and also where it is sensitive. How to remember the general recipe of the kernel trick: one, only inner products; two, replace inner products by K; three, express the solution as a linear combination of the training points; the weight vector never needs to be computed. Next, the following page turns to Extension: logistic bound.

steps.label: Extension: logistic bound
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the exponential loss punishes hardest. This extension asks which of the four losses are really upper bounds of the 0/1 loss. Hinge and exponential are never below the 0/1 loss; but at z equal to 0 the logistic is only ln 2, which is 0.693 and below 1, under the step of the 0/1 loss, so it is not an upper bound. After dividing by ln 2 it is exactly 1 at z equal to 0 and at least 1 for z at most 0, which makes it a convex upper bound of the 0/1 loss, called the normalized logistic loss in the source. Check: at z equal to −2, 2.127 divided by 0.693 is 3.069; at z equal to −1, 1.313 divided by 0.693 is 1.895, both above 1. Next, the following page turns to Extension: exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the logistic loss divided by ln 2 is a convex upper bound of the 0/1 loss. This page is the exercises, using the four points of the hand trace: points 1,0 and −1,0 are the positive class, points 0,1 and 0,−1 the negative class, the kernel K is x transpose z plus 1, squared, and alpha equals 1,1,1,1. Exercise 1: using the four kernels, compute g of x at x equal to 1,2: which class is it? Exercise 2: simplify g into an expression in x1 and x2 and check exercise 1. Work them out first; the next page is the worked solution. Next, the following page turns to Extension: worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two exercises. Exercise 1: the four kernel values at x equal to 1,2 are K with 1,0 equal to 4, with −1,0 equal to 0, with 0,1 equal to 9 and with 0,−1 equal to 1; the sum of alpha i y i is 0; so g is 4 plus 0 minus 9 minus 1 plus 0, which is −6, the negative class. Exercise 2: adding the four squares, g of x is 2 times x1 squared plus 1, minus 2 times x2 squared plus 1, which is 2 times x1 squared minus x2 squared; x equal to 1,2 gives 2 times 1 minus 4, which is −6, the same as exercise 1. Check: g above 0 means the absolute value of x1 exceeds that of x2, which goes to the positive class; the boundary is two diagonal lines, and the four points that no line could separate are separated by the kernel perceptron. This is the last page of KP20; the next KP is the following unit of chapter 4.
